front: What is the pull-quote thesis of Protic et al.'s DSM survey?
back: That the reduced cost of parallel software development will help make the DSM paradigm a viable solution to large-scale, high-performance computing.
source: Front matter (title, abstract, authors)

front: How does Protic et al. characterize the scope of their survey?
back: As "not exhaustive" but an "extensive, up-to-date overview of several key implementation schemes".
source: Front matter (title, abstract, authors)

front: What two-way classification of systems does the paper open with that the lesson does not state?
back: Shared-memory systems (tightly coupled multiprocessors with a global physical memory equally accessible to all processors) versus distributed-memory systems (multicomputers with independent nodes, local memory, and a general interconnection network).
source: Shared-memory vs distributed-memory background (the dichotomy the lesson skips)

front: According to the paper, what are the benefits and drawbacks of shared-memory systems?
back: Benefit: a convenient uniform read/write programming model that cuts software development cost. Drawbacks: contention, longer latencies, limited scalability, and complex memory-system design.
source: Shared-memory vs distributed-memory background (the dichotomy the lesson skips)

front: According to the paper, what are the benefits and drawbacks of distributed-memory systems?
back: Benefit: they scale well. Drawbacks: a message-passing model with explicit send/receive, the programmer must handle data distribution and communication, and process migration is complicated by distinct address spaces.
source: Shared-memory vs distributed-memory background (the dichotomy the lesson skips)

front: What is the paper's one-line summary of the shared- vs distributed-memory trade-off?
back: Compared with shared-memory systems, "hardware problems are easier and software problems more complex in distributed-memory systems"; DSM exists to combine the two.
source: Shared-memory vs distributed-memory background (the dichotomy the lesson skips)

front: What does DSM inherit from each of its two parent paradigms, per the paper?
back: From shared memory: programming ease and portability (preserving software investment). From distributed memory: scalability and cost-effectiveness.
source: Shared-memory vs distributed-memory background (the dichotomy the lesson skips)

front: In the paper's general DSM structure, what can a single cluster be, and why are private caches described as "virtually inevitable"?
back: A cluster can be a uniprocessor or a bus-organized multiprocessor; private caches are "virtually inevitable" for reducing latency.
source: General DSM system structure

front: In the paper's general DSM structure, how does a cluster's local memory relate to the global address space, and how is the cluster attached to the network?
back: Each cluster's local memory maps partially or entirely into the DSM global address space. A per-cluster interconnection controller attaches it to the network regardless of topology (bus, ring, mesh, or LAN).
source: General DSM system structure

front: Where do the state and current location of data blocks live in the paper's general DSM structure?
back: In a system table or directory.
source: General DSM system structure

front: Why does the paper call directory storage and organization one of the most important DSM design decisions?
back: Because it greatly affects system scalability.
source: General DSM system structure

front: What range of directory organizations does Protic et al. describe?
back: From full-map to dynamic structures (single/double-linked lists, trees); the directory can be flat or hierarchical, and centralized or distributed across clusters.
source: General DSM system structure

front: In the paper's hierarchical DSM topologies, what may intermediate-level clusters hold?
back: Only directories and interface controllers (no data); directory semantics depend on the consistency-maintenance method used.
source: General DSM system structure

front: What are the three design axes the paper organizes the DSM field around?
back:
1. How the access executes: the DSM algorithm.
  2. Where the mechanism is implemented: the implementation level.
  3. What "consistent" means: the memory consistency model.
source: The three design axes

front: What two basic problems does a DSM algorithm solve, per the paper?
back: Static and dynamic distribution of shared data to minimize access latency, and preserving a coherent view while minimizing coherence overhead.
source: DSM algorithms (the lesson's "access algorithm" section, in far more depth)

front: How does the paper precisely define replication vs migration, and when is each used?
back: Replication: multiple copies in different memories/caches, used mainly for simultaneous reads when read sharing prevails. Migration: a single copy that must be moved to the requesting site for exclusive use, preferred when sequential write-sharing patterns prevail.
source: DSM algorithms (the lesson's "access algorithm" section, in far more depth)

front: In SRSW algorithms, what is the stance on replication and migration?
back: Replication is prohibited; migration is permitted but not required.
source: Single reader/single writer (SRSW)

front: What is the simplest SRSW algorithm, and what is its main drawback?
back: The central server: one server services all requests to data physically on it. It is a bottleneck and implies no physical distribution.
source: Single reader/single writer (SRSW)

front: How does the modified central-server SRSW algorithm locate the server?
back: It statically distributes memory and server responsibility, using a mapping function such as hashing to locate the server.
source: Single reader/single writer (SRSW)

front: Why does the paper call the hot-potato SRSW algorithm's performance "restrictively low" and "rarely used"?
back: Because it cannot exploit parallel read-only copies.
source: Single reader/single writer (SRSW)

front: What is MRSW also called, and why are its algorithms "usually invalidation-based"?
back: Read-replication. A write to a writable copy is costly because stale copies must be prevented from use, so MRSW algorithms are usually invalidation-based.
source: Multiple reader/single writer (MRSW)

front: Define the paper's three MRSW terms: manager, owner, copy set.
back:
• Manager: site responsible for organizing write access to a block.
  • Owner: site owning the only writable copy.
  • Copy set: all sites holding copies.
source: Multiple reader/single writer (MRSW)

front: How does Li and Hudak's centralized manager MRSW algorithm work?
back: All read/write requests go to the manager (the only site knowing the owner); it forwards to the owner, waits for confirmation, and for writes sends invalidations to every site in the copy set.
source: Multiple reader/single writer (MRSW)

front: How does the improved centralized manager MRSW algorithm differ from the basic one?
back: The owner, not the manager, keeps the copy set, which travels with the data to the new owner, who performs invalidations; decentralized synchronization improves performance.
source: Multiple reader/single writer (MRSW)

front: How does the fixed distributed manager MRSW algorithm work, and when does it outperform centralized ones?
back: Each site manages a predetermined subset of blocks by a default mapping (overridable by clients); it outperforms centralized solutions under a high request rate.
source: Multiple reader/single writer (MRSW)

front: How does the broadcast distributed manager MRSW algorithm work, and what is its cost?
back: No manager; a requester broadcasts to find the true owner, which acts as manager and keeps the copy set. Cost: every processor must process each broadcast, slowing its own work.
source: Multiple reader/single writer (MRSW)

front: How does the dynamic distributed manager ("Li's algorithm") track ownership?
back: Each block tracks a probable owner rather than the real one; requests chase the probable-owner chain, and probable-owner fields update on every request/forward/invalidation.
source: Multiple reader/single writer (MRSW)

front: How does the dynamic distributed manager (Li's algorithm) scale as processors contend, and what variant distributes invalidation?
back: Performance degrades only logarithmically as processors contend; a tree-structured copy-set variant distributes invalidation responsibility.
source: Multiple reader/single writer (MRSW)

front: What is MRMW also called, and what update mechanism and coherence profile does it have?
back: Full-replication: replicated blocks with read and write permission, updates distributed to all copies by multicast/broadcast; appropriate for write sharing, often with write-update protocols; can produce high coherence traffic when update frequency and replica count are high.
source: Multiple reader/multiple writer (MRMW)

front: What coherence technique does the paper describe for MRMW using a sequencer?
back: Globally sequence writes via reliable multicast through a sequencer that assigns sequence numbers; a site receiving an out-of-order modification requests retransmission.
source: Multiple reader/multiple writer (MRMW)

front: What is the consistency property of the distributed-sequencer MRMW variant?
back: The master-copy server sequences writes per data structure; the system is then not sequentially consistent, but each structure stays individually consistent.
source: Multiple reader/multiple writer (MRMW)

front: What does the Shrewd algorithm do, and when is its benefit largest?
back: An enhancement of Li's algorithm that eliminates unnecessary page transfers using a per-copy sequence number: on a write fault at a node with a read-only copy, if its sequence number matches the owner's, the page need not be transferred. Benefit is large as the read-to-write ratio rises.
source: Avenues for performance improvement (entirely absent from the lesson)

front: What is the competitive replication/migration approach, and what guarantee does it give?
back: Replicate a remote page only when accesses exceed replication cost; migration has a stricter, access-pattern-dependent condition. Performance is guaranteed within a constant factor of optimal.
source: Avenues for performance improvement (entirely absent from the lesson)

front: How does the paper summarize the evolution from early to recent DSM?
back: Early DSM found gains in table organization (copy set) and management distribution; recent DSM relaxes consistency semantics, uses hardware accelerators, and combines invalidate and update methods.
source: Avenues for performance improvement (entirely absent from the lesson)

front: What two tasks does every DSM access require, and what three implementation groups result?
back: A lookup to decide whether data is local, and (on a write) an action to preserve coherence. Both can run in software, hardware, or a combination, giving three groups.
source: Implementation level (software / hardware / hybrid)

front: What is the basic trade-off of software DSM versus hardware DSM, per Protic et al.?
back: Software is more flexible and can tailor the consistency model to application behavior, but usually cannot match hardware performance. Relaxed consistency helps close the gap but burdens the programmer.
source: Software DSM implementations (none of these systems are in the lesson)

front: Why is software DSM grain size typically around a kilobyte, and what is the downside of coarse pages?
back: Management is done through virtual memory and page faults, so larger grain sizes (around a kilobyte) are typical. Coarse pages help high-locality applications and cut directory storage but hurt fine-grain-sharing programs through false sharing and thrashing.
source: Software DSM implementations (none of these systems are in the lesson)

front: What was IVY, and on what platform did it run?
back: One of the first software DSM systems: user-level modules on a modified Aegis OS on Apollo Domain workstations.
source: Software DSM implementations (none of these systems are in the lesson)

front: What coherence policy and page size did IVY use?
back: Invalidation on 1-Kbyte pages.
source: Software DSM implementations (none of these systems are in the lesson)

front: Which three sequential-consistency manager algorithms did IVY implement?
back: The improved centralized manager, the fixed distributed manager, and the dynamic distributed manager.
source: Software DSM implementations (none of these systems are in the lesson)

front: What speedup did IVY reach, and what was its main contribution?
back: Near-linear speedup up to eight clusters; its contribution was proving that DSM is viable.
source: Software DSM implementations (none of these systems are in the lesson)

front: What was distinctive about Mermaid, and on what machines and software layer did it run?
back: It was the first heterogeneous DSM (HDSM), spanning Sun/Unix workstations and DEC Firefly multiprocessors, implemented as a user-level library plus minor SunOS kernel changes.
source: Software DSM implementations (none of these systems are in the lesson)

front: How did Mermaid handle heterogeneity in its shared pages?
back: Data-conversion routines between machine types, one data type per page, and a variable page size.
source: Software DSM implementations (none of these systems are in the lesson)

front: What performance result does Protic et al. report for Mermaid?
back: Speedup increased by less than 20% when moving from DSM to physically shared memory (Firefly comparison, up to four nodes).
source: Software DSM implementations (none of these systems are in the lesson)

front: What coherence approach did Munin use, and how close did it get to hand-coded message passing?
back: Type-specific coherence plus release consistency; the programmer annotates each shared object with an access-pattern type (read-only, migratory, write-shared, producer-consumer, etc.) selecting a coherence protocol. It came within 10% of hand-coded message passing.
source: Software DSM implementations (none of these systems are in the lesson)

front: What consistency model did TreadMarks use, and at what level was it implemented?
back: Lazy release consistency; user-level, using Unix standard libraries with no kernel or compiler changes.
source: Software DSM implementations (none of these systems are in the lesson)

front: What write scheme did TreadMarks use?
back: Multiple-writer invalidation with a twin/diff scheme: copy (twin) a page on its first write, and compute a diff against the twin later.
source: Software DSM implementations (none of these systems are in the lesson)

front: What performance result does Protic et al. report for TreadMarks?
back: Good speedups for five Splash programs on DECstation-5000/240s over ATM and Ethernet.
source: Software DSM implementations (none of these systems are in the lesson)

front: What is distinctive about Midway's consistency support?
back: It supports multiple consistency models (processor, release, entry) switchable dynamically; shared data is explicitly associated with a synchronization object; sequential consistency is available if all shared accesses are properly labelled; uses an update mechanism; near-linear speedups on ATM.
source: Software DSM implementations (none of these systems are in the lesson)

front: What are the three variants of Blizzard, and which is most efficient?
back: Blizzard-S (software, insert a check routine before each shared reference), Blizzard-E (uses ECC bits to mark invalid blocks, MMU page protection for read-only), and Blizzard-ES (combination). Blizzard-S is most efficient (within a factor of two); slowdown of several times vs the KSR1 hardware DSM.
source: Software DSM implementations (none of these systems are in the lesson)

front: How does Mirage, an OS-kernel DSM, serve page requests?
back: It uses a page-segmentation model: all requests go to the segment-creation "library site" and queue sequentially there, and a "Clock site" supplies the most recent copy of the page.
source: Software DSM implementations (none of these systems are in the lesson)

front: In Clouds, what access attributes do objects have, and what risk does "weak-read" carry?
back: Objects of segments have attributes read-only/read-write/weak-read/none. Weak-read gives a copy with no guarantee against concurrent modification, so unrestricted use leads to inconsistent DSM.
source: Software DSM implementations (none of these systems are in the lesson)

front: In Clouds, how are segments fetched and synchronized, and where does that code live?
back: A DSM controller (DSMC) provides get and discard operations to fetch segments, plus P and V semaphore primitives; the DSMC is part of the Clouds OS but implemented outside its kernel Ra.
source: Software DSM implementations (none of these systems are in the lesson)

front: How does Linda model DSM, and how does it avoid the consistency problem?
back: As a "tuple space", a pool of user-defined tuples addressed by logical name, with operators to insert/remove/read tuples. It avoids the consistency problem by removing a tuple before update and reinserting the modified version.
source: Software DSM implementations (none of these systems are in the lesson)

front: What model does Orca (Bal and Tanenbaum) use for distributed programming?
back: A shared-data-object model (passive objects accessed through predefined operations) with selective replication, migration, and update; variant update mechanisms depending on the underlying communication (point-to-point, reliable/unreliable multicast).
source: Software DSM implementations (none of these systems are in the lesson)

front: How does hardware DSM manage shared data, per Protic et al.?
back: It replicates shared data in local memories and caches transparently to software, supporting fine-grain sharing at cache-line granularity, as an extension of scalable cache-coherence schemes.
source: Hardware DSM implementations (the lesson's hardware section, taxonomized)

front: What performance benefits does hardware DSM bring, per Protic et al., and at what cost?
back: It reduces communication and the effects of false sharing and thrashing, and speeds search and directory functions; the cost is design and verification complexity.
source: Hardware DSM implementations (the lesson's hardware section, taxonomized)

front: How does the paper characterize CC-NUMA?
back: A shared virtual address space statically distributed across local memories, accessible by all but with non-uniform latency; directory-based (full-map to dynamic); invalidation-based coherence; relaxed models for performance.
source: Hardware DSM implementations (the lesson's hardware section, taxonomized)

front: What is Memnet?
back: A ring-based "Memory as Network Abstraction"; the address space maps onto a reserved area of each local memory NUMA-style, plus a cache area for 32-byte remote blocks; coherence in hardware state machines; ring snooping satisfies misses from the nearest valid copy.
source: Hardware DSM implementations (the lesson's hardware section, taxonomized)

front: What does Dash stand for, and how are its clusters organized?
back: Directory Architecture for Shared Memory; 4-processor clusters, each owning part of the memory and of the directory.
source: Hardware DSM implementations (the lesson's hardware section, taxonomized)

front: How does Dash cache remote data, and how deep is its memory hierarchy?
back: Two-level private caches hold remote 16-byte blocks, within a four-level memory hierarchy.
source: Hardware DSM implementations (the lesson's hardware section, taxonomized)

front: What kind of directory does Dash use, and with which block states?
back: A full-map directory with block states uncached, cached, and dirty.
source: Hardware DSM implementations (the lesson's hardware section, taxonomized)

front: What consistency model and optimizations does Dash use?
back: Release consistency plus software-visible prefetch, update, and deliver optimizations, and hardware synchronization support.
source: Hardware DSM implementations (the lesson's hardware section, taxonomized)

front: What is SCI, and how does it organize its directory?
back: The IEEE P1596 Scalable Coherent Interface standard (an interface standard, not a full design); it distributes the directory among sharing caches as doubly linked lists; the home keeps only a head pointer and status bits; read misses chain the requester as the new list head; writes invalidate down the list.
source: Hardware DSM implementations (the lesson's hardware section, taxonomized)

front: What proposed enhancements does the paper list for SCI?
back: Sharing trees, request combining, and queue-based locks.
source: Hardware DSM implementations (the lesson's hardware section, taxonomized)

front: How does the paper characterize COMA?
back: Local memories act as huge caches ("attraction memories") with no fixed home; data is replicated/migrated on demand; a hierarchical network topology simplifies locating blocks and replacement; less sensitive to static data distribution than NUMA but higher remote-miss latency and storage overhead.
source: Hardware DSM implementations (the lesson's hardware section, taxonomized)

front: What is the KSR1's topology and local memory, and what routes its requests?
back: A ring-based hierarchy with a 32-Mbyte local cache per node; the "Allcache engine" routes requests through the hierarchy.
source: Hardware DSM implementations (the lesson's hardware section, taxonomized)

front: What are the KSR1's allocation and transfer units?
back: Allocation unit: a 16-Kbyte page. Transfer and sharing unit: a 128-byte subpage.
source: Hardware DSM implementations (the lesson's hardware section, taxonomized)

front: What coherence protocol and states does the KSR1 use?
back: An invalidation protocol with states exclusive, nonexclusive, copy, and invalid, plus an atomic state for synchronization.
source: Hardware DSM implementations (the lesson's hardware section, taxonomized)

front: Why is cache-line replacement complicated in the KSR1?
back: Because, as a COMA machine, it has no main-memory home for data.
source: Hardware DSM implementations (the lesson's hardware section, taxonomized)

front: What are the defining features of the DDM (Data Diffusion Machine)?
back: 4-processor clusters with attraction memory and a split-transaction bus; a set-associative directory holding state (no data) for items below it; snoopy write-invalidate; seven item states (invalid/exclusive/valid plus four transient).
source: Hardware DSM implementations (the lesson's hardware section, taxonomized)

front: How does a reflective memory system (RMS) share data, per Protic et al.?
back: Shared segments are mapped through programmable tables and selectively "reflected" across clusters; it is full-replication MRMW, with each write broadcast or multicast in hardware, at fine granularity, to all clusters holding the address. It resembles write-update cache coherence.
source: Hardware DSM implementations (the lesson's hardware section, taxonomized)

front: What read and write performance properties does a reflective memory system have?
back: The processor does not stall on writes, and all reads are local with deterministic access time.
source: Hardware DSM implementations (the lesson's hardware section, taxonomized)

front: What are the features of the RMS (Encore) reflective-memory system?
back: Bus-based, a write-only RM bus carrying word-based writes (address + value); later Memory Channel adds block updates; an 8-Kbyte replication segment treated as a window that can be open (reflected) or closed.
source: Hardware DSM implementations (the lesson's hardware section, taxonomized)

front: What are the features of Merlin?
back: Mesh-based reflective memory with word-granularity sharing; OS calls initialize routing maps; the interface noninvasively copies each shared write and multicasts it; two sharing modes, synchronous (through a canonical cluster) and rapid (shortest routes); supports heterogeneous processing.
source: Hardware DSM implementations (the lesson's hardware section, taxonomized)

front: How does Plus divide DSM work between software and hardware?
back: Software handles data placement and replacement in 4-Kbyte pages; hardware handles write-update coherence at 32-bit-word granularity.
source: Hybrid-level DSM implementations (whole category absent from the lesson)

front: How does Plus organize the replicas of a page?
back: Replicas are chained in a singly linked list headed by the master copy.
source: Hybrid-level DSM implementations (whole category absent from the lesson)

front: How does Plus handle write ordering?
back: Writes are nonblocking; the user issues a "fence" when strong ordering is needed.
source: Hybrid-level DSM implementations (whole category absent from the lesson)

front: What are Plus's "delayed operations"?
back: Read-modify-write operations split into an issue phase and a verify phase.
source: Hybrid-level DSM implementations (whole category absent from the lesson)

front: How does Galactica Net split work between software and hardware, and what page states does it use?
back: On-demand page replication under Mach VM software, plus a hardware block-transfer engine; page states are read-only, private, and update.
source: Hybrid-level DSM implementations (whole category absent from the lesson)

front: How does Galactica Net propagate writes to shared pages?
back: Hardware write-update over a "virtual sharing ring".
source: Hybrid-level DSM implementations (whole category absent from the lesson)

front: When does Galactica Net switch coherence policy, and how does it decide?
back: It can switch dynamically from hardware update to software invalidate when remote updates dominate, using per-page update counters.
source: Hybrid-level DSM implementations (whole category absent from the lesson)

front: What is the LimitLESS directory protocol in MIT Alewife?
back: Hardware directory entries hold a limited number of pointers, with software (via interrupt and fast trap) emulating a full-map directory in the rare overflow cases; a multiple-context concept hides latency.
source: Hybrid-level DSM implementations (whole category absent from the lesson)

front: What is distinctive about Flash's coherence implementation?
back: A software coherence protocol executed on an auxiliary "Magic" protocol processor rather than the main CPU, pipelined, avoiding main-processor context switches; it also supports low-overhead message passing.
source: Hybrid-level DSM implementations (whole category absent from the lesson)

front: What is Typhoon, and what is its "Stache" library?
back: Proposed hardware for the Tempest interface (low-overhead messages, bulk transfer, VM management, fine-grain access control); a network-interface processor dispatches user-level handlers. The "Stache" user library replicates remote data COMA-style at page granularity, with coherence at block level.
source: Hybrid-level DSM implementations (whole category absent from the lesson)

front: What is Shrimp, and what is AURC?
back: Reflective memory with a virtual-memory-mapped network interface doing automatic update in hardware; AURC (automatic update release consistency) keeps one copy consistent by fine-grain automatic update and others by software invalidation; it also uses "scope consistency", a compromise between entry and lazy release consistency.
source: Hybrid-level DSM implementations (whole category absent from the lesson)

front: What is cooperative shared memory / CICO?
back: Programmer Check-In/Check-Out annotations as performance primitives that do not change semantics even if misapplied; supported by a minimal directory protocol Dir1SW.
source: Hybrid-level DSM implementations (whole category absent from the lesson)

front: What hybrid protocol combines a Midway-like software part with directory-based hardware, and what does its variable-size unit eliminate?
back: A hybrid combining a Midway-like software part for coarse-grain regions (BeginRead/EndRead, BeginWrite/EndWrite annotations) with directory-based hardware for fine-grain, both invalidation-based; the variable-size software coherence unit eliminates false sharing.
source: Hybrid-level DSM implementations (whole category absent from the lesson)

front: How do Alewife and Flash illustrate the convergence of message passing and shared memory?
back: Alewife allows explicit message sends in a shared-memory program; Flash adds low-overhead message passing with protection.
source: Hybrid-level DSM implementations (whole category absent from the lesson)

front: How does the paper define a memory consistency model, and what is the stronger-vs-looser trade-off?
back: It defines the legal ordering of memory references issued by a processor as observed by other processors. Stronger models raise latency and bandwidth needs but simplify programming; looser models improve performance at the cost of programmer effort to synchronize.
source: Memory consistency models (the section to check against the lesson hardest)

front: How does the paper split consistency models by their treatment of synchronization accesses?
back: Into models that treat synchronization accesses as ordinary (sequential, processor) and models that distinguish them (weak, release, lazy release, entry).
source: Memory consistency models (the section to check against the lesson hardest)

front: How does the paper define sequential consistency (Lamport), and where does it hold?
back: All processors observe the same interleaving of reads/writes issued in sequences by individual processors; a simple implementation is a single-port memory serializing a FIFO queue, or a DSM central server serializing requests, with no bypassing of same-processor requests. It holds in most bus-based multiprocessors and early DSM (IVY, Mirage).
source: Memory consistency models (the section to check against the lesson hardest)

front: How does the paper define release consistency, and who implements it?
back: It splits synchronization into acquire and release: ordinary accesses may run only after prior acquires on the same processor, a release only after prior ordinary reads/writes complete, and acquire/release accesses must meet processor-consistency requirements. Dash and Munin implement it differently.
source: Memory consistency models (the section to check against the lesson hardest)

front: How does entry consistency improve on release consistency, and who first implemented it?
back: It requires every ordinary shared variable/object to be associated with a synchronization variable, so an acquire propagates only the subset that variable guards; this gives lower latency (a shared access need not wait on unrelated acquires) but higher programmer burden. Midway first implemented it.
source: Memory consistency models (the section to check against the lesson hardest)

front: Beyond the three axes, what six characteristics does the paper list as strongly affecting DSM performance?
back: Cluster configuration, interconnection network, structure of shared data, coherence-unit granularity, DSM-management responsibility, and coherence policy.
source: Important design choices (a checklist the lesson gives only piecemeal)

front: What does the paper say about cluster configuration as a design choice?
back: Off-the-shelf processors have their own caches, so cluster-level cache coherence must integrate with the DSM mechanism; local memory is split private/shared; the NIC sometimes carries DSM management duties.
source: Important design choices (a checklist the lesson gives only piecemeal)

front: What does the paper say about the interconnection network as a design choice?
back: Most software DSM is network-independent (often Ethernet); hardware DSM uses multilevel buses, ring hierarchies, meshes; topology affects parallel data exchange, scalability, and the cost of broadcast/multicast.
source: Important design choices (a checklist the lesson gives only piecemeal)

front: How does the paper contrast hardware vs software handling of the shared data structure?
back: Hardware deals with non-structured objects; software uses logical data items to exploit application locality.
source: Important design choices (a checklist the lesson gives only piecemeal)

front: How does the paper frame centralized vs distributed DSM-management responsibility?
back: Centralized is easy but a bottleneck; distributed (static or dynamic) is scalable; the choice is closely tied to directory distribution.
source: Important design choices (a checklist the lesson gives only piecemeal)

front: How does the paper advise choosing between update and invalidate coherence policies?
back: For very fine-grain data an update costs about the same as an invalidation, so word-based systems favour update and coarse-grain systems favour invalidation; invalidation is better when read/write sequences to a datum are not highly interleaved; the best policy adapts dynamically to reference patterns.
source: Important design choices (a checklist the lesson gives only piecemeal)

front: What is the paper's overall conclusion about DSM's maturity?
back: DSM is a viable solution for large-scale high-performance systems with reduced parallel-software cost, but commercial systems are "in their infancy" and research prototypes still prevail.
source: Conclusion and research directions

front: What research directions does the paper list as promising?
back: Improving/adapting algorithms to applications and configurations; synergistic hardware-software combination; integrating shared-memory and message-passing paradigms; new memory-system architectures; and combining multiple consistency models.
source: Conclusion and research directions
